questions.question: How do you approach a Low-Level Design interview from start to finish?
questions.title: How to Approach an LLD Interview
questions.direct_answer: Treat an LLD interview as a **scaled-down system design with code-level detail**. Follow a fixed sequence: **(1) clarify requirements** (functional + non-functional + scope), **(2) identify entities and relationships**, **(3) sketch the class diagram** (responsibilities, interfaces, key methods), **(4) walk through one or two flows**, **(5) write code for the critical classes** (interfaces, core method bodies — not getters/setters), **(6) discuss concurrency, extensibility, edge cases, and trade-offs**. Avoid jumping to code. Use **interfaces + composition** rather than deep inheritance. Apply SOLID without naming it. Drive the conversation — the interviewer is checking how you decompose, not whether your code compiles.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can structure an open-ended OO design problem, decompose responsibilities, choose the right abstractions, and reason about extensibility / concurrency under time pressure.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Jumping straight to code without clarifying scope; modeling the world (50 classes) instead of the problem; deep inheritance hierarchies; forgetting concurrency and edge cases.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Structured flow with explicit clarifying questions, named SOLID/pattern usage where it earns its keep, concurrency and extensibility discussion, and code that's clean even at the signature level.

sections.title: What LLD Interviews Actually Test
sections.content:
An LLD interview gives you a deliberately under-specified problem ("design a parking lot", "design Splitwise") and ~45-60 minutes. The interviewer is **not** checking:

- Whether your code compiles.
- Whether you remember every GoF pattern by name.
- Whether you cover every edge case in the world.

They **are** checking:

- How you **structure ambiguity** — do you ask clarifying questions or build assumptions silently?
- How you **decompose** — do you find the right entities, the right boundaries between them?
- How you **abstract** — interfaces, composition, polymorphism used where they earn their keep.
- How you **reason about change** — what extensions you anticipate, what hot spots will need to evolve.
- How you **handle concurrency** — because most realistic systems have it.
- How you **communicate** — do you drive the conversation or wait to be asked?

A strong candidate sounds like a senior engineer thinking out loud, not like a textbook reciting principles.

sections.title: The Six-Step Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR R[1. Clarify
requirements] --> E[2. Identify
entities] E --> C[3. Class
diagram] C --> F[4. Walk
through flows] F --> CO[5. Code
critical bits] CO --> X[6. Concurrency,
extensibility,
trade-offs] ``` **Time budget (45 min):** - Clarify: 5-7 min - Entities + relationships: 5 min - Class diagram: 10 min - Walk-through: 5 min - Code: 12-15 min - Trade-offs / extensions: 5 min If you spend 30 minutes on code and never clarified requirements, you've failed before you started.

sections.title: Step 1 — Clarify Requirements
sections.content:
Three buckets to ask about, in order:

**Functional scope** — what's in / out:
- 'Single parking lot or multi-floor / multi-location?'
- 'Reservations or walk-in only?'
- 'Payment in scope?'
- 'Multiple vehicle types and sized spots?'

**Non-functional / scale:**
- 'Single instance or distributed?'
- 'Concurrent users?'
- 'In-memory only, or do we persist state?'

**Out-of-scope confirmation:**
- 'I'll skip authentication / billing infra unless you want it modeled.'

**Why this matters:** every clarifying question rules out a different class hierarchy. Designing for 'one lot, in-memory' is a totally different design than 'multi-region, persistent, with reservations'.

**Write the agreed scope down** (top of whiteboard / shared editor) so you and the interviewer can refer back to it.

sections.title: Step 2 — Identify Entities and Relationships
sections.content:
Pull the **nouns** out of the problem statement and the requirements. For a parking lot:

- `ParkingLot`, `Floor`, `Spot`, `Vehicle`, `Ticket`, `EntryGate`, `ExitGate`, `PaymentProcessor`, `RateStrategy`.

Then the **verbs** (these become methods or use cases):

- 'park vehicle', 'unpark vehicle', 'compute fee', 'find spot'.

Then **relationships:**

- `ParkingLot` *has many* `Floor`s.
- `Floor` *has many* `Spot`s.
- `Spot` *has zero or one* `Vehicle`.
- `Ticket` *references* a `Spot` and a `Vehicle` and an entry time.

Get enough to draw a quick block diagram. Don't model the universe — only what your scoped problem requires.

sections.title: Step 3 — Sketch the Class Diagram
sections.content:
Draw classes + key fields + key methods. Mermaid (or plain ASCII / whiteboard) is fine.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        +park(vehicle) Ticket
        +unpark(ticket) Receipt
    }
    class Floor {
        +findAvailableSpot(type) Spot
    }
    class Spot {
        +SpotType type
        +assign(vehicle)
        +release()
    }
    class Vehicle
    class Ticket
    class FeeStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +calculate(ticket) Money
    }

    ParkingLot --> Floor
    Floor --> Spot
    Spot --> Vehicle
    ParkingLot --> FeeStrategy
```

**Heuristics for good class shapes:**
- One responsibility per class (SRP).
- Vary-by-policy bits behind an interface (Strategy) — fee calculation, spot allocation.
- Composition over inheritance (`Spot` *has a* `SpotType`, not `CarSpot extends Spot`).
- Abstract interfaces named for the role (`FeeStrategy`, `SpotAllocator`), not the implementation (`HourlyFeeImpl`).
- Identify the **interfaces and ports** before concrete classes.

sections.title: Step 4 — Walk Through a Flow
sections.content:
Pick the most representative flow and walk through it explicitly:

> 'Vehicle arrives → EntryGate calls `parkingLot.park(vehicle)` → lot picks a `Floor` → floor finds available `Spot` for that vehicle's `SpotType` via `SpotAllocator` → spot is `assign`ed to the vehicle → `Ticket` is created with entry time and spot reference → returned to caller. On exit: `parkingLot.unpark(ticket)` → spot is `release`d → `FeeStrategy.calculate(ticket)` runs → receipt returned.'

The walk-through:
- **Validates your design** — you'll catch missing classes / wrong responsibilities here.
- **Lets the interviewer interject** with constraints or twists.
- **Communicates clearly** — they see your design 'animated' instead of static.

sections.title: Step 5 — Code the Critical Pieces
Step 6 — Concurrency, Extensibility, Trade-offs
sections.content:
Bring this up before the interviewer asks. Three buckets:

**Concurrency:**
- 'Two vehicles arriving simultaneously — we need atomic spot reservation. Either synchronize spot lookup + assignment, or use `ConcurrentHashMap` with `compute()` for atomic check-and-set on the spot.'
- 'For multi-floor, partition by floor and lock per floor to reduce contention.'

**Extensibility:**
- 'New spot types? Add to `SpotType` enum (or `SpotType` interface for open polymorphism); existing code unchanged.'
- 'Different pricing models? `FeeStrategy` is the extension point.'
- 'Reservations later? Add a `ReservationService` that pre-reserves spots; lot's `park()` checks for held reservations first.'

**Trade-offs:**
- 'I used Strategy for fees; alternative is a rule engine, but Strategy is simpler for this scope.'
- 'I'm using in-memory state; for persistence we'd add a `LotRepository` and persist on assign/release — but that opens up consistency questions.'

This is where senior candidates separate themselves — showing you understand the **shape of future change**.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Jumping to code first.** Half your hour gone, no shared understanding.
- **Modeling the universe.** 50 classes for a parking lot. Stick to your scope.
- **Deep inheritance.** `Vehicle ← Car ← SedanCar ← LuxurySedanCar`. Use composition + enums / strategies.
- **God classes.** A 30-method `ParkingService` doing fee calculation, spot allocation, ticketing.
- **Ignoring concurrency.** Single-threaded code in a problem that's obviously concurrent.
- **Naming patterns out loud as a flex.** 'I'll use the Decorator + Visitor + Composite + Chain-of-Responsibility patterns.' Pick patterns that earn their keep; don't pile them on.
- **Refusing to make decisions.** 'It depends' is fine *once*; then commit, build, and call out the alternative.
- **No interface boundaries.** Hard-coded `HourlyFee` in the lot — you can't even mock it for tests.
- **Skipping the walk-through.** Diagrams without flows hide design holes.
- **Not asking the interviewer for input.** It's a conversation; ask 'does this match what you had in mind?' at decision points.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Six-step flow:** clarify → entities → class diagram → walk-through → code critical pieces → concurrency/extensibility/trade-offs.
- **Time-box each step;** don't get stuck in one phase.
- **Clarify scope first** — functional, non-functional, and what's out.
- **Identify nouns, then verbs, then relationships.**
- **Composition over inheritance;** interfaces named for the role.
- **Apply SOLID where it earns its keep,** not as a recitation.
- **Code the critical 1-2 methods,** skip boilerplate.
- **Always discuss concurrency and future extensions** before they ask.
- **Drive the conversation;** check in at decision points.
- **The interviewer is grading how you think,** not your code's compilability.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**What LLD interviews test**

Deliberately under-specified problem, 45-60 min. Interviewer not checking whether code compiles, whether you remember every GoF pattern, every edge case.

They are checking: how you structure ambiguity, decompose, abstract (interfaces, composition, polymorphism where they earn their keep), reason about change (extensions, evolution hotspots), handle concurrency, communicate.

Strong candidate sounds like a senior engineer thinking out loud, not a textbook reciting principles.

**Six-step flow**

1. Clarify requirements (5-7 min)
2. Identify entities + relationships (5 min)
3. Class diagram (10 min)
4. Walk through flows (5 min)
5. Code critical bits (12-15 min)
6. Concurrency, extensibility, trade-offs (5 min)

If you spend 30 min on code and never clarified requirements, you've failed before you started.

**Step 1 — clarify**

Three buckets, in order:

Functional scope: in/out. 'Single lot or multi-floor/location?' 'Reservations or walk-in only?' 'Payment in scope?' 'Multiple vehicle types and sized spots?'

Non-functional / scale: 'Single instance or distributed?' 'Concurrent users?' 'In-memory only, or persist state?'

Out-of-scope confirmation: 'I'll skip auth/billing infra unless you want it modeled.'

Every clarifying question rules out a different class hierarchy. Write agreed scope down at top of whiteboard.

**Step 2 — entities and relationships**

Nouns from problem: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, EntryGate, ExitGate, PaymentProcessor, RateStrategy.

Verbs (→ methods or use cases): park vehicle, unpark, compute fee, find spot.

Relationships: ParkingLot has many Floors. Floor has many Spots. Spot has zero or one Vehicle. Ticket references Spot + Vehicle + entry time.

Don't model the universe — only what your scope requires.

**Step 3 — class diagram**

Classes + key fields + key methods. Mermaid or whiteboard.

Heuristics:
- One responsibility per class (SRP)
- Vary-by-policy bits behind interface (Strategy) — fee calculation, spot allocation
- Composition over inheritance (Spot has a SpotType, not CarSpot extends Spot)
- Abstract interfaces named for role (FeeStrategy, SpotAllocator), not implementation (HourlyFeeImpl)
- Identify interfaces / ports before concrete classes

**Step 4 — walk through a flow**

Pick the most representative flow and walk through:

Vehicle arrives → EntryGate calls parkingLot.park(vehicle) → lot picks a Floor → floor finds available Spot for that vehicle's SpotType via SpotAllocator → spot is assigned to vehicle → Ticket created with entry time + spot reference → returned. On exit: parkingLot.unpark(ticket) → spot released → FeeStrategy.calculate(ticket) runs → receipt returned.

Walk-through validates design (you'll catch missing classes), lets interviewer interject, communicates 'animated' design.

**Step 5 — code the critical pieces**

Don't write every class. Write:
- Interfaces for strategy / extension points
- 1-2 methods driving the flow — parkingLot.park(), feeStrategy.calculate()
- Enums if they clarify (SpotType, VehicleType, OrderStatus)

Skip getters/setters/constructors/toString/exception bodies. Say 'standard boilerplate' and move on.

**Step 6 — concurrency, extensibility, trade-offs**

Bring up before interviewer asks.

Concurrency: two vehicles arriving simultaneously — atomic spot reservation. Synchronize spot lookup + assignment, or ConcurrentHashMap with compute() for atomic check-and-set. For multi-floor, partition by floor, lock per floor to reduce contention.

Extensibility: new spot types — add to enum or interface for open polymorphism. Different pricing — FeeStrategy is the extension point. Reservations later — ReservationService that pre-reserves; lot.park() checks held reservations first.

Trade-offs: 'I used Strategy for fees; alternative is a rule engine, but Strategy is simpler for this scope.' 'In-memory state; for persistence we'd add LotRepository and persist on assign/release — but opens consistency questions.'

This separates senior candidates — showing you understand shape of future change.

**Common mistakes**

- Jumping to code first
- Modeling the universe (50 classes for a parking lot)
- Deep inheritance (Vehicle ← Car ← SedanCar ← LuxurySedanCar)
- God classes (30-method ParkingService)
- Ignoring concurrency
- Naming patterns out loud as a flex
- Refusing to make decisions ('it depends' for everything)
- No interface boundaries (hard-coded HourlyFee — can't mock for tests)
- Skipping the walk-through
- Not asking interviewer for input — it's a conversation

**Recommendation**

**Treat the LLD interview as a structured conversation, not a coding sprint. Spend the first 15 minutes on clarification + entities + class diagram before you write any code. Use composition + interfaces for variability points (Strategy for fees, Allocator for spot finding); avoid deep inheritance and god classes. Code only the critical 1-2 methods and the strategy interfaces — skip boilerplate. Always close with a concurrency analysis, two extension scenarios, and one trade-off you consciously made. Drive the conversation — ask the interviewer for input at every major decision point.**

followup_questions: How would you adapt this flow if the interview is 30 minutes instead of 60?
When is it correct to skip the class diagram and go straight to code?
How do you handle an interviewer who keeps adding requirements halfway through?
How do you decide what to code vs leave as 'pseudo-code with a comment'?

questions.question: How do you apply SOLID and composition over inheritance in real LLD problems?
questions.title: Applying SOLID and Composition in LLD Problems
questions.direct_answer: SOLID isn't a checklist to recite — it's a set of forces that shape good OO design. **In real LLD problems**: keep classes single-purpose (**SRP**); allow new behavior without modifying existing classes via interfaces and Strategy/Factory (**OCP**); ensure subclasses honor their supertype's contract (**LSP**); split fat interfaces into role-specific ones (**ISP**); depend on abstractions not concrete classes (**DIP**). **Prefer composition over inheritance** — a `Vehicle` has a `EngineType` instead of `ElectricCar extends Car`. Inheritance for *true 'is-a'* relationships only; composition for *behavior variation*. The result: classes are small, swappable, testable in isolation, and extensible without breaking existing code.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you apply SOLID as design forces (not as recited bullet points), and whether you reach for composition before inheritance for behavior variation.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating SOLID as a five-item to-do list to mention; using inheritance as the default tool for 'reuse' (creating fragile hierarchies).
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show concrete refactors from violation → fix; talk about LSP via the Rectangle/Square problem; show composition replacing a 4-level hierarchy with a 2-level + interface.

sections.title: Why SOLID and Composition Matter in LLD
sections.content:
Most LLD interview anti-patterns come from two failures:

1. **Mixing responsibilities** — one class does too much, so changes ripple unpredictably (violates SRP, OCP).
2. **Inheriting for code reuse** — deep `extends` chains where subclasses can't substitute their parents (violates LSP, makes change risky).

SOLID is the named set of constraints that prevent these. Composition over inheritance is the structural choice that makes the constraints easy to honor. Together they produce designs that are:

- **Small** — each class understandable in seconds.
- **Swappable** — implementations live behind interfaces; testing with mocks/fakes is trivial.
- **Extensible** — new behavior added without modifying existing code.
- **Local** — a change in one class doesn't ripple to ten others.

The interviewer doesn't want to hear 'I will follow SOLID.' They want to see you make decisions consistent with it as you go.

sections.title: S — Single Responsibility Principle
O — Open/Closed Principle
L — Liskov Substitution Principle
I — Interface Segregation Principle
D — Dependency Inversion Principle
Composition Over Inheritance — The Bigger Lever
sections.content:
Inheritance is the heaviest coupling tool in OO. A subclass inherits everything: fields, methods, behavior, exceptions, threading assumptions. Reaching for `extends` should be a deliberate decision.

**Inheritance is appropriate when:**
- True **is-a** relationship that satisfies LSP.
- The subclass should be substitutable everywhere the parent is.
- The behavior is genuinely shared and stable (`AbstractList` → `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`).

**Composition is appropriate when:**
- You're adding **behavior variation** (different fee strategies, different discount rules).
- You want to **swap** at runtime.
- You want to **combine** behaviors.

**Example — inheritance trap:**
```java
class Vehicle { ... }
class Car extends Vehicle { ... }
class ElectricCar extends Car { ... }
class LuxuryElectricCar extends ElectricCar { ... }
class AutonomousLuxuryElectricCar extends LuxuryElectricCar { ... }
```
Four levels deep. What if a vehicle is autonomous but not electric? You can't combine traits.

**Composition fix:**
```java
class Vehicle {
    private final EngineType engine;          // PETROL, ELECTRIC, HYBRID
    private final ComfortLevel comfort;       // STANDARD, LUXURY
    private final AutonomyLevel autonomy;     // MANUAL, AUTONOMOUS
}
```
One class, three independent variation axes. Any combination is expressible. Adding a new axis (e.g., `BodyStyle`) is one more field, not a hierarchy explosion.

For more behavioral composition, use interfaces:
```java
class Vehicle {
    private final DrivetrainBehavior drivetrain;   // ElectricDrivetrain, PetrolDrivetrain
    private final ParkingBehavior   parking;       // ManualParking, AutonomousParking
}
```
Swappable at construction time. Easy to test in isolation.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **SOLID as a recitation.** Mentioning the names without showing the design force is theatre.
- **Inheritance as default.** Reaching for `extends` for code reuse rather than for true 'is-a' relationships.
- **Deep hierarchies.** More than 2-3 levels of `extends` is almost always a smell.
- **Subclasses overriding to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.** Classic LSP red flag.
- **God interfaces.** A `UserService` with 25 methods; clients only ever use 3.
- **Field injection (`@Autowired` on a field).** Hides dependencies; breaks immutability; harder to test.
- **'I'll add an interface later if needed.'** Usually you won't; the concrete dependency leaks everywhere.
- **Interfaces for everything.** YAGNI — don't introduce a one-implementation interface 'just in case'. Add it when the second implementation appears.
- **Open/Closed taken too literally.** Sometimes editing existing code is the right answer; OCP is a guideline, not a religion.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **SRP:** one reason to change per class.
- **OCP:** new behavior via new implementations, not edits to existing code.
- **LSP:** subclasses must honor the parent's contract; if not, they're not really 'is-a'.
- **ISP:** small role-specific interfaces; clients depend only on what they use.
- **DIP:** depend on abstractions; constructor-inject concrete dependencies.
- **Composition over inheritance** for behavior variation; inheritance only for true 'is-a' + LSP-honoring relationships.
- **Strategy + interface** is the workhorse pattern — it satisfies OCP, ISP, DIP simultaneously.
- **Avoid recitation;** show SOLID through the design choices you make.
- **YAGNI moderates SOLID** — don't introduce abstraction without a concrete reason.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**Why SOLID and composition matter**

Most LLD anti-patterns come from two failures:

1. Mixing responsibilities — one class does too much, changes ripple unpredictably (violates SRP, OCP)
2. Inheriting for code reuse — deep extends chains, subclasses can't substitute parents (violates LSP, makes change risky)

SOLID is the named set of constraints that prevent these. Composition over inheritance is the structural choice making them easy to honor. Result: classes small, swappable, extensible, local in change.

Interviewer doesn't want to hear 'I will follow SOLID.' Wants to see decisions consistent with it as you go.

**S — SRP**

One class, one reason to change.

Violation: Order class with place(), calculateTax(), sendConfirmationEmail(), persistToDb(), exportToCsv(). Four different reasons to change.

Fix: Order (state + place/cancel), TaxCalculator, OrderConfirmationMailer, OrderRepository, OrderExporter. Each changes for one reason. Use case orchestrates.

**O — OCP**

Open for extension, closed for modification. Mechanism: interface + new implementation.

Violation: PaymentProcessor.pay() with if/else if for credit_card, paypal, upi, crypto. Every new method edits existing code.

Fix: PaymentMethod interface. CreditCardPayment, PaypalPayment, UpiPayment implement it. New method = new file, never edit existing. Critical when existing code has dozens of dependents and tests.

**L — LSP**

Subclasses must honor parent's contract.

Classic violation: Square extends Rectangle. setWidth forces height; setHeight forces width. resize(Rectangle r) that sets width=5, height=10 expects area=50 — fails for Square (100).

Fix: don't model square as rectangle. Both implement Shape with area().

Practical heuristic: subclass overrides to throw UnsupportedOperationException or behaves differently from documented expectations → LSP violated; inheritance is wrong.

**I — ISP**

Don't force clients to depend on methods they don't use. Many small role-specific interfaces beat one fat interface.

Violation: Worker interface with work(), eat(), sleep(). Robot.eat() throws UnsupportedOperationException.

Fix: split by role. Workable, Eatable, Sleepable. Human implements all three; Robot implements Workable only.

LLD application: keep repository/gateway/strategy interfaces focused. UserRepository with 30 methods hard to mock; signals some methods belong elsewhere. UserFinder, UserUpdater, UserDeleter often cleaner.

**D — DIP**

Depend on abstractions, not concretions.

Violation: OrderService with private MySqlOrderRepository = new MySqlOrderRepository(). Can't unit-test without MySQL. Can't swap DB. Can't decorate mailer with retries.

Fix: OrderRepository + EmailSender interfaces. OrderService constructor takes them. Adapters implement them. Tests pass fakes. Production wires real ones via Spring.

Constructor injection is canonical Java mechanism. Avoid field injection (hides dependencies, breaks immutability).

**Composition over inheritance — the bigger lever**

Inheritance is the heaviest coupling tool in OO. Subclass inherits everything. Reaching for extends should be deliberate.

Inheritance appropriate when: true is-a satisfying LSP, subclass substitutable everywhere parent is, behavior genuinely shared and stable (AbstractList → ArrayList).

Composition appropriate when: adding behavior variation, swapping at runtime, combining behaviors.

Inheritance trap: Vehicle ← Car ← ElectricCar ← LuxuryElectricCar ← AutonomousLuxuryElectricCar. Four levels deep. Autonomous but not electric? Can't combine traits.

Composition fix: Vehicle has EngineType, ComfortLevel, AutonomyLevel. Three independent variation axes. Any combination expressible. New axis = one more field, not hierarchy explosion.

For behavioral composition: DrivetrainBehavior + ParkingBehavior interfaces. Swappable at construction time. Easy to test in isolation.

**Common mistakes**

- SOLID as recitation — mentioning names without showing design force
- Inheritance as default — extends for reuse rather than true is-a
- Deep hierarchies — more than 2-3 levels almost always a smell
- Subclasses overriding to throw UnsupportedOperationException — LSP red flag
- God interfaces — UserService with 25 methods; clients use 3
- Field injection — hides dependencies, breaks immutability, harder to test
- 'I'll add an interface later if needed' — usually you won't; concrete dependency leaks everywhere
- Interfaces for everything — YAGNI; add when second implementation appears
- OCP taken too literally — sometimes editing existing code is right; OCP is guideline, not religion

**Recommendation**

**Apply SOLID as design forces, not as a checklist. Single responsibility per class; new behavior via new implementations of stable interfaces (Strategy is the workhorse); subclasses that genuinely substitute their parents (otherwise prefer composition); small role-specific interfaces; depend on abstractions and constructor-inject concrete adapters. Default to composition for behavior variation; reserve inheritance for true is-a relationships that pass the Liskov test. YAGNI moderates everything — don't introduce abstraction without a concrete second use. The result is small, swappable, testable, and extensible classes — which is what an interviewer is grading.**

followup_questions: Refactor a 25-method `UserService` god class into ISP-compliant pieces.
Show how Strategy + DIP gives you a payment system that's extensible without edits.
When is inheritance the right tool, and what test do you apply?
How does YAGNI temper SOLID — give an example of over-engineering.

speakable_v2.hook: SOLID isn't a checklist to recite. It's the set of forces that show up when one class does too much — or when an inheritance chain breaks the moment a piece needs to swap.

beats.text: SOLID is five constraints — single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov substitution, interface segregation, dependency inversion. Composition is the structural choice that makes the constraints easy to honor.

Most LLD problems trip on the same shape — a class doing too much, joined to a deep extends chain where the subclass can't safely stand in for the parent. SOLID names that force; composition is the tool reached for first.

steps: SRP — one class, one reason to change. Order doesn't also calculate tax and send the email.
OCP — new behaviour as a new file, not an edit. Strategy interface, not an if-else chain in PaymentProcessor.
LSP — the subclass honors the parent's contract. Square extends Rectangle is the canonical violation; both should be Shape.
ISP — many small interfaces beat one fat one. A UserRepository with 30 methods is the smell.
DIP — depend on interfaces. OrderService takes OrderRepository, not MySqlOrderRepository. Constructor injection.

paragraphs: PaymentProcessor with an if-else over 'credit_card', 'paypal', 'upi'. Adding 'crypto' means editing and re-testing every existing branch. That's an OCP violation in the wild.

The refactor: one PaymentMethod interface, one class per method (CreditCardPayment, PaypalPayment, UpiPayment). Adding crypto becomes a new file — no edit to existing code, no regression risk on the methods that already work. The non-obvious win: the tests for credit_card never change again.

items: Reciting SOLID as five bullets without a refactor — the sharp signal someone's read the names, not used them.
Inheritance as the default tool for reuse — fragile hierarchies, LSP violations sneak in. Reach for composition first.
Splitting too eagerly — three classes for what could be one is just as hard to read. SRP says 'one reason to change', not 'one method'.
Field injection (@Autowired on a field) instead of constructor injection — hides the dependency list and breaks immutability.

speakable_v2.cap: SOLID's a noticing tool, not a recipe. The interviewer's listening for one thing — a refactor where the violation got spotted and fixed. Reach for composition first.

tts_overrides.MySqlOrderRepository: my S Q L order repository
